Rule.title: Ensure no duplicate UIDs exist
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Although the useradd program will not let you create a duplicate User ID (UID), it is possible for an administrator to manually edit the /etc/passwd file and change the UID field.
Rationale: Users must be assigned unique UIDs for accountability and to ensure appropriate access protections.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Based on the results of the audit script, establish unique UIDs and review all files owned by the shared UIDs to determine which UID they are supposed to belong to.

check.check-content: Run the following script and verify no results are returned: #!/bin/bash cut -f3 -d":" /etc/passwd | sort -n | uniq -c | while read x ; do [ -z "$x" ] && break set - $x if [ $1 -gt 1 ]; then users=$(awk -F: '($3 == n) { print $1 }' n=$2 /etc/passwd | xargs) echo "Duplicate UID ($2): $users" fi done

Rule.title: Ensure no duplicate GIDs exist
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Although the groupadd program will not let you create a duplicate Group ID (GID), it is possible for an administrator to manually edit the /etc/group file and change the GID field.
Rationale: User groups must be assigned unique GIDs for accountability and to ensure appropriate access protections.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Based on the results of the audit script, establish unique GIDs and review all files owned by the shared GID to determine which group they are supposed to belong to.

check.check-content: Run the following script and verify no results are returned: #!/bin/bash cut -d: -f3 /etc/group | sort | uniq -d | while read x ; do echo "Duplicate GID ($x) in /etc/group" done

Rule.title: Ensure no duplicate user names exist
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Although the useradd program will not let you create a duplicate user name, it is possible for an administrator to manually edit the /etc/passwd file and change the user name.
Rationale: If a user is assigned a duplicate user name, it will create and have access to files with the first UID for that username in /etc/passwd. For example, if "test4" has a UID of 1000 and a subsequent "test4" entry has a UID of 2000, logging in as "test4" will use UID 1000. Effectively, the UID is shared, which is a security problem.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Based on the results of the audit script, establish unique user names for the users. File ownerships will automatically reflect the change as long as the users have unique UIDs.

check.check-content: Run the following script and verify no results are returned: #!/bin/bash cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd | sort | uniq -d | while read x do echo "Duplicate login name ${x} in /etc/passwd" done

Rule.title: Ensure no duplicate group names exist
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Although the groupadd program will not let you create a duplicate group name, it is possible for an administrator to manually edit the /etc/group file and change the group name.
Rationale: If a group is assigned a duplicate group name, it will create and have access to files with the first GID for that group in /etc/group. Effectively, the GID is shared, which is a security problem.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Based on the results of the audit script, establish unique names for the user groups. File group ownerships will automatically reflect the change as long as the groups have unique GIDs.

check.check-content: Run the following script and verify no results are returned: #!/bin/bash cut -d: -f1 /etc/group | sort | uniq -d | while read x do echo "Duplicate group name ${x} in /etc/group" done

Rule.title: Ensure shadow group is empty
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The shadow group allows system programs which require access the ability to read the /etc/shadow file. No users should be assigned to the shadow group.
Rationale: Any users assigned to the shadow group would be granted read access to the /etc/shadow file. If attackers can gain read access to the /etc/shadow file, they can easily run a password cracking program against the hashed passwords to break them. Other security information that is stored in the /etc/shadow file (such as expiration) could also be useful to subvert additional user accounts.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Remove all users from the shadow group, and change the primary group of any users with shadow as their primary group.

check.check-content: Run the following commands and verify no results are returned: # grep ^shadow:[^:]*:[^:]*:[^:]+ /etc/group # awk -F: '($4 == "<shadow-gid>") { print }' /etc/passwd

Rule.title: Ensure all users' home directories exist
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Users can be defined in /etc/passwd without a home directory or with a home directory that does not actually exist.
Rationale: If the user's home directory does not exist or is unassigned, the user will be placed in "/" and will not be able to write any files or have local environment variables set.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: If any users' home directories do not exist, create them and make sure the respective user owns the directory. Users without an assigned home directory should be removed or assigned a home directory as appropriate.

check.check-content: Run the following script and verify no results are returned: #!/bin/bash grep -E -v '^(halt|sync|shutdown)' /etc/passwd | awk -F: '($7 != "'"$(which nologin)"'" && $7 != "/bin/false") { print $1 " " $6 }' | while read -r user dir; do if [ ! -d "$dir" ]; then echo "The home directory ($dir) of user $user does not exist." fi done

Rule.title: Enable timeout support for login shells
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>When establishing an individual to a system ID, a login shell which supports time out must be used. The guidance from other sections in this benchmark is only sufficient for login shells: /bin/csh, /bin/tcsh, /bin/sh, /bin/ksh, /bin/ksh93, and /bin/bash. This guidance is also sufficient for /bin/sh when the concerned link is a symbolic or hard link to one of the previously listed shells. If other login shells are permitted, similar controls must be established. Where this is done, add it to the 'agreed to Value' column. Neither the bourne shell nor the dash shell support this control, and neither shell may be used as a login shell. Shells from /bin/false, /sbin/nologin, and other no-login shells are exempt from this requirement and are permitted. Additional no-login shells defined by the account can be added to the 'agreed to Value' column. The special-purpose shells from /bin/sync, /sbin/shutdown, and /sbin/halt are also exempt from this requirement, but must not be set as the login shell for an individual to a system ID. An individual logging in to system IDs must have one of the following shells set as login shell: /bin/csh, /bin/tcsh, /bin/sh, /bin/ksh, /bin/bash, /bin/sh, /bin/false, /sbin/nologin, /usr/bin/sh, /usr/bin/bash, /usr/sbin, /nologin, /bin/ksh93, or /usr/bin/ksh93.
Rationale: Having no timeout value associated with a shell could allow an unauthorized user access to another user's shell session (for example, the user walks away from their computer and does not lock the screen). Setting a timeout value at least reduces this risk.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Check if the indicated shell supports time out. If it does and the customer requires it's usage, update the technical specification 'agreed to values' to reflect this requirement. Be sure to update the 'default' requirements for setting timeout for the shell. That is, set systems to terminate a session after a period of inactivity as follows: PCI Servers = 15 minutes, or 900 seconds. GDPR Servers = 30 minutes, or 1800 seconds. HIPAA Servers = 30 minutes, or 1800 seconds. All other servers = 6 hours, or 21600 seconds. If the shell is to be permitted to the general population, add it to the shells in file /etc/shells. usermod --shell /bin/bash $Uid

check.check-content:
Run the following procedure: file=/etc/passwd Shells='/bin/csh|/bin/tcsh|/bin/sh|/bin/ksh|/bin/bash|/bin/sh|/bin/false| /sbin/nologin|/usr/bin/sh|/usr/bin/bash|/usr/sbin/nologin|/bin /ksh93|/usr/bin/ksh|/usr/bin/rksh|/usr/bin/ksh93|' cat $file | egrep -v '^sync:.:/bin/sync\s$|^halt:.:/sbin/halt\s$|^shutdown:. :/sbin/shutdown\s$' | while read ENTRY do SHELL=$(echo $ENTRY | awk -F: '{printf $7"
"}') Uid=$(echo $ENTRY | awk -F: '{printf $1"
"}') [[ "$SHELL" != @($Shells) ]] && printf " WARNING: Verify shell supports autologout/TMOUT function - id: $Uid - shell: $SHELL
" done This procedure should return nothing. Note: This procedure also passes without having defined shells, as Linux assigns an effective default shell /bin/sh to the ID.

Rule.title: Ensure correct assignment of cryptographic coprocessors and domains for EP11 tokens
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that for each openCryptoki EP11 token the correct set of cryptographic coprocessors and domains to be used by the token is assigned.
Rationale: An incorrect configuration can lead to the usage of a wrong cryptographic coprocessor for cryptographic operations.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Specify the correct assignment of cryptographic coprocessors and domains for each EP11 token as described in Defining an EP11 token-specific configuration file.

check.check-content: Check the set of assigned cryptographic coprocessor and domains for each available openCryptoki EP11 token in the appropriate EP11 token-specific configuration files.

Rule.title: Ensure correct control domain assignment
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>When managing cryptographic devices on the Trusted Key Entry (TKE) workstation, the operating system needs access to control domains. Ensure that control domains are only assigned to LPARs that are allowed to manage master keys within a hardware security module (HSM).
Rationale: Unauthorized change of HSM master keys can weaken or disable cryptographic operations performed by other systems.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Change the assignment of control domains via the HMC (Hardware Management Console). See Hardware Management Console Operations Guide. Download the PDF and navigate to topic: Tasks -> HMC Tasks -> Change LPAR Cryptographic Controls.

check.check-content: On the Hardware Management Console (HMC), make sure that control domains are only assigned to LPARs that need to manage cryptographic devices via the TKE workstation.

Rule.title: Ensure access to cryptographic devices is allowed only through device nodes created by zcryptctl
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>In containerized environments, ensure that access to cryptographic devices is only allowed through multi device node extensions created by with the correct assignment of cryptographic coprocessors and domains.
Rationale: Assigning all host cryptographic devices to a container allows the containerized workload unwanted arbitrary access to cryptographic resources.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: For each container create additional crypto devices as described in zcryptctl - Control access to AP queues and functions

check.check-content: Enter the following command: zcryptctl list Ensure that each container is assigned a specific device node with the correct assignment of cryptographic coprocessors and domains.

Rule.title: Configure redundant APQNs and make sure they are on different adapters
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>When performing cryptographic operations, it is recommended to provide redundant cryptographic resources (that is, APQNs) on different physical cryptographic adapters.
Rationale: If the cryptographic coprocessors (adapters) are not redundant, the system is more susceptible to hardware failure. Also, the ability to perform hardware-supported cryptographic operations at all may get lost.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Configure additional APQNs for the system by adding adapters and domains the the LPAR on the HMC (Hardware Management Console). See Hardware Management Console Operations Guide. Download the PDF and navigate to topic: Tasks -> HMC Tasks -> Change LPAR Cryptographic Controls.

check.check-content: Enter the following command: lszcrypt CARD.DOMAIN TYPE MODE STATUS REQUESTS ---------------------------------------------- 08 CEX7C CCA-Coproc online 4 08.0031 CEX7C CCA-Coproc online 4 09 CEX7C CCA-Coproc online 2 09.0031 CEX7C CCA-Coproc online 2 0a CEX7P EP11-Coproc online 0 0a.0031 CEX7P EP11-Coproc online 0 Verify that APQNs are available on different adapters (different values in the CARD column).

Rule.title: Enable CPACF feature
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>It is recommended to enable the CP Assist for Cryptographic Functions (CPACF) feature when performing supported cryptographic operations.
Rationale: Without CPACF enabled, cryptographic operations for supported algorithms are not accelerated by the hardware, thus reducing overall workload performance.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Enable CPACF on the Hardware Management Console (HMC). See Hardware Management Console Operations Guide. Download the PDF and navigate to topic: Tasks -> HMC Tasks -> Customize/Delete Activation Profiles -> CP Assist for Cryptographic Functions.

check.check-content: Enter the following command: # icainfo In the resulting output, make sure that for the value in column hardware > static reads yes for the relevant cryptographic algorithms, as shown in the following sample excerpt: Cryptographic algorithm support ------------------------------------------------------ | hardware | function | dynamic | static | software ---------------+------------+------------+------------ SHA-1 | no | yes | yes SHA-224 | no | yes | yes ... SHA-512/224 | no | yes | yes SHA-512/256 | no | yes | yes ... AES ECB | no | yes | yes AES CBC | no | yes | yes AES OFB | no | yes | no ... ------------------------------------------------------

Rule.title: Ensure cio_ignore is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>When a Linux on Z instance boots, it senses and analyzes all available I/O devices. You can use the cio_ignore command to specify devices that are to be ignored. So ensure that cio_ignore is used to only make required channel devices available.
Rationale: Using devices inadvertently can lead to data corruption or leaks.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Add cio_ignore=all to the kernel command line in the boot loader entry in /boot/loader/entries. Then run the zipl command and restart the system.

check.check-content: Enter the following command to display specifications for all devices that are not in the current exclusion list, that is, they are currently not ignored: cio_ignore -L Make sure that only devices are listed that are required for the current workload. Additionally enter the following command: grep cio_ignore=all /proc/cmdline In the resulting output, verify that all devices are ignored by default on system boot. For example: # grep cio_ignore=all /proc/cmdline root=/dev/disk/by-path/ccw-0.0.1c80-part1 crashkernel=128M rd.dasd=0.0.1c80 rd.dasd=0.0.1c83 cio_ignore=all``,!condev rd.znet=qeth,0.0.bdf0,0.0.bdf1, 0.0.bdf2,layer2=1,portno=0 BOOT_IMAGE=0

Rule.title: Enable SMART monitor
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that the SMART monitor is enabled to be notified of disk issues in order to prevent silent disk failures.
Rationale: Without monitoring SMART events for disk devices, errors leading to disk failures can not be identified and disk devices can fail before being replaced.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: To enable the SMART monitor service, enter the following command: systemctl enable --now smartd.service

check.check-content: Enter the following command to ensure that the smartd.service is enabled and running: systemctl status smartd.service

Rule.title: Configure dm-crypt to use XTS-PAES with 256 bit keys
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>When using full disk encryption via dm-crypt, it is recommended to use the XTS-PAES cipher mode with 256 bit keys.
Rationale: A key length of 256 bits is required to ensure future-proof quantum-safe encryption. Using the XTS-PAES cipher mode results in a much smaller passphrase making key management easier for the user.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Reformat the device using cryptsetup luksFormat and specify --cipher xts-paes and --key-size 256. See also: Pervasive Encryption

check.check-content: Enter the following command to verify the cipher mode: $ cryptsetup luksDump <device> | grep -E "^Cipher mode|^MK bits" Cipher mode: xts-paes MK bits: 256

Rule.title: Ensure UID uniqueness checking is active
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Activate UID uniqueness checking to ensure stable addressing for Peripheral Component Interconnect (PCI) devices.
Rationale: Deactivating or activating a PCI device can change its corresponding PCI domain, resulting in a change of the NIC (network interface cardname) device in the operating system. This can compromise security for mechanisms that rely on the NIC, like for example, iptables.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: UID uniqueness checking can be enabled in the IOCDS.

check.check-content: Read the uid_is_unique attribute for any PCIe device that is available to your Linux instance to find out which naming scheme applies. Example: # cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:00:00.0/uid_is_unique 1 If the value is 1, UID uniqueness checking is enabled, and the network interface names are based on UIDs. For any other value, UID uniqueness checking is not enabled, and the network interface names are based on FIDs.

Rule.title: NVMe setting for data resilience
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>When using NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory express) devices for disk storage, it is recommended to implement redundancy over multiple devices via software RAID for data resilience.
Rationale: NVMe devices do not have built-in hardware capabilities for redundancy similar to classic IO devices (DASD, zfcp). Therefore, redundancy needs to be implemented at the software level. Without redundancy, disk failure of a single disk can lead to data loss.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Configure software RAID across redundant devices either via block device level or file system level mechanisms.

check.check-content: To check software RAID at block device level, enter the following command: lsblk In the output, verify that the mount point of the specific file system is distributed across redundant physical devices, for example: NAME MAJ:MIN RM SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINT dasda 94:0 0 20.6G 0 disk `-dasda1 94:1 0 20.6G 0 part / dasdb 94:4 0 20.6G 0 disk `-dasdb1 94:5 0 20.6G 0 part [SWAP] To check software RAID at file system level, use the utilities specific for the used file system to show information about the RAID status, for example, for the Btrfs (B-Tree filesystem): $ btrfs filesystem show /mnt/ Label: none uuid: 46c3b60c-9abe-41b9-9d4e-efd3da0c059a Total devices 2 FS bytes used <size> devid 1 size <path> used <size> path <path> devid 2 size <path> used <size> path <path> In the resulting output, verify that the file system is distributed across redundant physical devices.

Rule.title: Ensure that unused PCI Devices are disabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>In general it is recommended to keep unused PCI (Peripheral Component Interconnect) devices disabled so that for example, NICs (Network Interface Card) are not used inadvertently.
Rationale: Inadvertent usage of devices can lead to data corruption or leakage.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Enter the following command to detach the devices in the IOCDS: echo 0 >/sys/bus/pci/slots/<slot>/power This ensures that any events are no longer processed by the effected hardware.

check.check-content: Enter the following command: lspci Make sure that only devices are listed in the resulting output, that are required for the current workload.

Rule.title: Configure SMC-D for network traffic isolation
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>When using Shared Memory Communication - Direct Memory Access (SMC-D) networking, it is recommended that each SMC-D device belongs to a different virtual channel ID (VCHID).
Rationale: All SMC-D devices belonging to the same VCHID might be able to eavesdrop traffic.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Configure individual SMC-D devices to have different VCHIDs.

check.check-content: Use the smc_rnics tool to list, enable and disable (R)NICs as used by SMC-R and SMC-D. Make sure that each SMC-D device has a unique physical channel identifier (PCHID) value.

Rule.title: Ensure RoCE card redundancy settings are configured properly
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>When using channel-bonding over multiple RoCE NICs, it is recommended that each PCI function ID (FID) belongs to a different support partition on the CEC.
Rationale: If the support partition is shared between PCI FIDs in the same bond, and that support partition becomes unavailable (for example, by an upgrade procedure), the whole channel bond becomes unavailable.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark
reference.dc:subject: CIS RHEL8 on IBM Z Linux Benchmark

Rule.fixtext: Support partitions for PCI FIDs can only be configured via changes in the IOCDS data set.

check.check-content: Enter the following command: cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/<addr>/pfip/segment0 Make sure that the value for the PCI support partition is different for all RoCE devices.
